question.prompt:
Let \(S\) be the set of points on the rays forming the sides of a \(120^\circ\) angle, and let \(P\) be a fixed point inside the angle on the angle bisector. Consider all distinct equilateral triangles \(PQR\) with \(Q\) and \(R\) in \(S.\) (Points \(Q\) and \(R\) may be on the same ray, and switching the names of \(Q\) and \(R\) does not create a distinct triangle.) solutions.explanation:
To choose E, it is enough to construct infinitely many distinct triangles; we do not need to classify every possible triangle.

Let O be the vertex of the angle. Call its two sides the upper and lower rays, as displayed. Choose A on the upper ray and B on the lower ray so that OA=OB=OP. Since OP bisects the 120° angle, \(\angle AOP=\angle POB=60^\circ\). Each of triangles OAP and OBP therefore has two equal sides with included angle 60°, so both are equilateral.

Now rotate about P counterclockwise through 60°. The two equilateral triangles show that this rotation sends O to B and A to O. Consequently, it sends the whole segment OA onto the segment BO.

Choose any Q strictly between O and A, and let R be its image under this rotation. Then R lies strictly between B and O, so Q and R belong to the required rays. Rotation gives \(PQ=PR\) and \(\angle QPR=60^\circ\), making PQR equilateral.

There are infinitely many choices of Q on the open segment OA. Each resulting triangle has exactly one vertex on the upper ray and one on the lower ray, so different choices of Q give different triangles even when exchanging the names Q and R is allowed. Thus there are infinitely many such triangles, and the answer is \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
solutions.title: Rotate a segment between the rays

solutions.explanation:
Coordinates let us verify a whole family of triangles by checking their three side lengths. Choose the unit of length to be OP, put the angle vertex at \(O=(0,0)\), and put \(P=(1,0)\). Each boundary ray makes a 60° angle with the positive horizontal axis. The 30°–60°–90° triangle ratios therefore give the rays as \(y=\sqrt3x\) and \(y=-\sqrt3x\), with \(x\geq0\).

For any real number \(t\) satisfying \(0<t<\tfrac12\), choose
\[
Q=(t,\sqrt3t),\qquad
R=\left(\tfrac12-t,-\sqrt3\left(\tfrac12-t\right)\right).
\]
Both horizontal coordinates are positive, so Q and R lie on opposite rays. Using squared distances avoids unnecessary square roots:
\[
PQ^2=(1-t)^2+3t^2=4t^2-2t+1,
\]
\[
PR^2=\left(\tfrac12+t\right)^2+3\left(\tfrac12-t\right)^2
=4t^2-2t+1,
\]
and
\[
QR^2=\left(2t-\tfrac12\right)^2+\left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)^2
=4t^2-2t+1.
\]
Thus all three side lengths are equal. The points are distinct because Q is strictly above the horizontal axis, R is strictly below it, and P is on it. Hence PQR is an equilateral triangle.

The interval \(0<t<\tfrac12\) contains infinitely many numbers. Different values give different upper-ray vertices Q, so they give distinct triangles even without naming Q and R. This family alone proves that there are infinitely many triangles, and the answer is \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
solutions.title: Construct a family with equal distances
